Revelation 17:10: "five have fallen, the one is" (WEB). On the Julian count, the sixth king was Nero.
John 19:15: the chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar!" (WEB).

Many preterists agree on Rome but read the land beast as the imperial cult and its local priests in Asia. Most scholars of all schools take this view. Futurists see a future world ruler and a false prophet. Historicists often see papal Rome.
Why count 666 in Hebrew rather than Greek or English?
Because John writes Greek but thinks in Hebrew. He gives Hebrew names in Revelation and his Gospel, so his readers would naturally try Hebrew letters.

R. H. Charles, a major commentator on Revelation, said that John writes in Greek but thinks in Hebrew. The book itself switches languages. The angel of the abyss is named in Hebrew, Abaddon, and in Greek, Apollyon (9:11). Armageddon is a Hebrew place name (16:16). In John's Gospel, the Pavement is also called by its Hebrew name, Gabbatha (John 19:13), and the sign on the cross was written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (19:20). Moving from Greek to Hebrew was normal for John and his Jewish-Christian readers. In contrast, modern solutions in English could not have been intended by John, since English did not exist then.
Revelation 9:11: "In Hebrew, his name is Abaddon, but in Greek, he has the name Apollyon" (WEB).
John 19:20: the title on the cross was "written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek" (WEB).

Some scholars argue that readers in Greek-speaking Asia would count in Greek, as Irenaeus did. Others take 666 as a triangular number, or as the Greek value of "beast" (thērion) written in Hebrew letters (also 666). They see the number as theological rather than a name.
How does the name "Nero Caesar" equal 666?
Written in Hebrew as Neron Qesar (נרון קסר), the letters total 50 + 200 + 6 + 50 + 100 + 60 + 200 = 666. This spelling is found in ancient sources.

Hebrew has no separate number symbols. Its letters carry values. The Greek form "Neron Kaisar" written in Hebrew letters is nrwn qsr. The values are nun 50, resh 200, vav 6, nun 50, qof 100, samekh 60, resh 200. The total is 666. This spelling is not a modern invention. A document from Wadi Murabba'at (Mur 18), dated to the second year of Nero, spells his name in this way, and the form also appears in rabbinic sources. The beast is called "a man" (13:18). Nero was feared and despised as a persecutor. On the fulfilled reading, a Jewish Christian who tried his name in Hebrew would have found the answer quickly.
Mur 18, an Aramaic document from about AD 55/56, is dated "year two of Nero Caesar" with this spelling.

Many scholars across schools accept Nero as the best first-century solution, including some who date Revelation late (they link it to the "Nero returning" legend). Futurists object that the method needs the spelling to be chosen. They see Nero at most as a type of a future beast.
Why do some ancient manuscripts read 616 instead of 666?
Probably because the Latin form "Nero Caesar" (without the final n) in Hebrew letters totals 616. A copyist who knew the Nero solution may have adjusted the number.

Irenaeus already knew copies reading 616 around AD 180 (Against Heresies 5.30.1). A papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (P115, about AD 225-275) also reads 616. Bruce Metzger, a leading textual scholar, suggested a reason. "Neron Caesar" in Hebrew letters is 666, while the Latin form "Nero Caesar" (nrw qsr) drops one nun (50) and gives 616. A scribe used to the Latin form may have "corrected" the number to keep it pointing to Nero. If so, the variant is early evidence that Christians linked the number to Nero. Both spellings point to the same man. Scribes copied by hand and sometimes changed what they thought was a mistake.
666 minus nun (50) = 616. This is the exact difference between "Neron" and "Nero".
Papyrus 115 (Oxyrhynchus), one of the oldest copies of Revelation 13, reads 616.
Scholars agree that 666 is the better reading. Not all accept that 616 arose from the Nero spelling; some think it was an accident or another calculation. Irenaeus himself thought 616 was an error.
Did Nero fit the beast in character and deeds?
Yes, in key ways. He was the first emperor to persecute Christians, he made war on the saints, he died by the sword, and Rome then recovered from near collapse.

After the fire of Rome in AD 64, Nero blamed the Christians. Tacitus says they were torn by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches at night (Annals 15.44). Church tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul under Nero. This matches the beast making war on the saints (13:7). The beast's power lasts forty-two months (13:5). Nero killed his own mother, Agrippina. He died in June AD 68 by putting a blade to his own throat (Suetonius, Nero 49), compare 13:10 and 13:14. One of the heads seemed mortally wounded, yet the beast lived (13:3). After Nero's death, the empire nearly fell apart in civil war, then revived under Vespasian. The world "marvelled" at Rome's recovery.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Christians were put to death "with every kind of mockery".
AD 68-69: Galba, Otho and Vitellius all fell within a year. Vespasian then restored order, and the "wound" of the empire healed.

Some scholars link 13:3 instead to the "Nero redivivus" legend that Nero would return. Futurists see the healed wound as a future ruler's apparent resurrection. Others note that Nero's persecution was largely limited to Rome, while Revelation addresses Asia.
Did early Christian writers connect the beast with Nero?
Many did connect the beast with Nero or a Roman emperor. Victorinus and Commodian linked it to a returning Nero, and Augustine reported the view.

Early Christian writers did not agree on one answer, but Rome and Nero appear again and again. Irenaeus (about AD 180) suggested Lateinos, the Roman power. Victorinus of Pettau (died about 304), in the earliest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation, linked the beast of chapter 17 to Nero raised again. Commodian, Lactantius and Sulpicius Severus also mention Nero's return. Augustine recorded that some held Nero would rise or return as Antichrist (City of God 20.19). The Sibylline Oracles (book 5) show that the Nero legend was widely known. F. W. Farrar summed it up: the earliest writers connected Nero or some emperor with the beast. The fulfilled reading sees this as support for a first-century answer.
Augustine, City of God 20.19: some suppose Paul's "mystery of lawlessness" refers to Nero.
Sibylline Oracles 5.137-154, a Jewish text of the late first or early second century, speaks of Nero fleeing and returning.

Futurists note that the early writers mostly expected a future Antichrist, sometimes a revived Nero, not a fulfilment already past. This supports a future reading, or at least a "Nero as type" reading, more than full fulfilment in AD 68.
Why does the number 666 appear with Solomon's gold?
In 1 Kings 10:14 Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year, just as he began breaking the king's law of Deuteronomy 17. Some see 666 as a mark of that turning away.

The number 666 appears in the Old Testament three times: Solomon's yearly gold (1 Kings 10:14; 2 Chronicles 9:13) and the sons of Adonikam who returned from exile (Ezra 2:13). Deuteronomy 17:16-17 told Israel's king not to multiply horses, wives or gold. 1 Kings 10-11 shows Solomon doing all three. He took horses from Egypt and many foreign wives, who turned his heart to other gods (11:1-4). Some readers, like James Jordan, see 666 as a sign of "apostate Solomon": a king of God's people bound to Gentile powers through trade and idolatry. Solomon's kingdom was torn after his death. On this reading, the leaders who rejected the Son of David also lost their kingdom in AD 70.
1 Kings 10:14: "the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents" (WEB).
Deuteronomy 17:17: the king "shall not greatly multiply to himself silver and gold" (WEB).

Most commentators do not think John meant to allude to Solomon, since Revelation 13:18 calls 666 the number of a man's name. Some idealists find a theological echo of wealth and idolatry, but they combine it with a symbolic or Roman reading.
How could the land beast look like a lamb but speak like a dragon?
It looked religious but served Satan's aims. On this reading, the leaders who rejected Jesus kept religious forms while working with Rome to persecute his followers.

The land beast has "two horns like a lamb" but speaks "as a dragon" (13:11). The dragon is Satan (12:9). It is not the dragon, but it speaks like him. Jesus told certain opponents that they were doing the desires of the devil, a liar and murderer (John 8:44). Revelation calls hostile groups in Smyrna and Philadelphia a "synagogue of Satan" (2:9; 3:9). Before Pilate, the chief priests said, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15). In Acts they brought charges against Paul before Roman governors (Acts 24:1-9). On the fulfilled reading, these are words about specific leaders and groups in a first-century dispute. They are never a judgment on Jewish people as a whole, and must not be used to justify hatred.
Acts 24:1: the high priest Ananias came with an orator to accuse Paul before Felix.
Matthew 7:15: false prophets come "in sheep's clothing" but inwardly are wolves. This is a similar picture.

Most scholars identify the land beast with the "false prophet" (16:13; 19:20). They see it as the imperial cult priesthood in Asia that promoted emperor worship. Futurists see a future religious leader. Many scholars warn that phrases like "synagogue of Satan" were misused in later anti-Jewish polemic and must be read in context.
Must we choose between Nero and the Solomon link for 666?
Not necessarily. On this reading, the sea beast (Rome under Nero) and the land beast (apostate leadership) worked together, so the number can echo both.

The two beasts of Revelation 13 cooperate. The land beast exercises the authority of the first beast and makes people worship it (13:12). If the sea beast is Rome under Nero, his name fits the count of 666. If the land beast is the leadership that sided with Rome, the echo of Solomon's 666 talents fits its apostasy. These leaders rejected the Son of David and followed the path of Solomon's later years, rather than that of his father David. This reading does not answer every question. But it keeps the interpretation within biblical theology and first-century history, rather than in the daily news. At least 1 Kings 10 is God's word.
Revelation 13:12: the second beast "exercises all the authority of the first beast" (WEB).
Luke 23:12: Herod and Pilate became friends on the day of Jesus's trial. This is an alliance of rulers against Christ, compare Psalm 2:2.

Most interpreters choose one primary solution, often Nero or a symbolic meaning. Some idealists, such as G. K. Beale, read 666 as a symbol of imperfection repeated three times. They see it as compatible with a historical echo but not reducible to one name.
Why are futurist identifications of the beast so hard to test?
Because if the beast appears only after the church is gone, no prediction can be checked by Christians. Failed claims are simply moved to the next candidate.

One popular writer said that knowing how to identify the Antichrist is of no practical use to the church, since believers will be watching from heaven when he appears. The same book still said that he is probably alive now. This shows a problem. If the beast and his mark come only after the rapture, Christians can never test the claims, and no claim can be proved wrong. Writers can say "could be" and "might", and adjust when events fail. The fulfilled reading accepts a harder test: its claims are tied to known history and must fit it. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gives a simple rule: a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the LORD.
Deuteronomy 18:22: if the thing does not happen, the prophet "has spoken it presumptuously" (WEB).
Each failed candidate, from Mussolini to Gorbachev, was dropped without a change to the system.

Careful futurists agree that naming candidates is unwise, and many condemn it. They answer that their view is testable in principle: the prophecies will be fulfilled literally in the future. Preterism, they say, must also stretch some details to fit AD 70.
Is the Antichrist alive somewhere in the world today?
On the fulfilled reading, no. John said many antichrists had already come in his "last hour", and nothing in Scripture points to one man alive in our time.

Hal Lindsey wrote in 1970, 1977 and 1980 that the Antichrist was alive somewhere. Dave Hunt said he was "almost certainly alive", probably a mature, admired politician. Lindsey also warned against guessing which world figure he is. He said it hardly matters, since Christians will be gone. The fulfilled reading answers from John, the only biblical writer to use the word. John told his readers that "even now many antichrists have arisen" (1 John 2:18), and that the spirit of antichrist was "already in the world" (4:3). The antichrists were present in the first century, not waiting in the twentieth or twenty-first. Christ's people should test spirits (4:1) rather than search the news for a hidden ruler.
1 John 2:18: "even now many antichrists have arisen. By this we know that it is the final hour" (WEB).
Claims since 1970 that the Antichrist was "alive now" have now run for over fifty years without any fulfilment.

Many futurists hold that a final personal Antichrist will come, though most responsible scholars refuse to say he is alive now. Historicists identify the Antichrist with a long-lasting system. Amillennial writers often expect a final antichrist figure at the end, while stressing that many antichrists are already here.
Have Christians in past centuries also claimed the Antichrist was already born?
Yes. Martin of Tours (died 397) said he had no doubt the Antichrist was already born. Modern claims repeat an old pattern that has always failed.

Sulpicius Severus records that Martin of Tours said the Antichrist had already been born and would gain supreme power when grown (Dialogues 2.14). That was over 1,600 years ago. In 1962 the American fortune-teller Jeane Dixon claimed a vision of a child born in the Middle East on 5 February 1962. She said he would unite all faiths by the end of the century. Her picture closely resembles modern prophecy teaching. Each generation has heard such assurances, and each was wrong. The fulfilled reading asks why Christians should trust today's forecasts after so many failures. It also asks whether such forecasts come from Scripture at all, or from a pattern of fear and speculation.
About AD 400: Martin of Tours is reported to say the Antichrist "has already been born".
1962: Jeane Dixon's vision of a world-uniting child. Her timeline of the 1980s and 1999 passed without fulfilment.
Futurists agree that past guesses failed and that date-setting is wrong. They say failed guesses do not disprove a future Antichrist, any more than false messiahs disproved the real Messiah.
Why is there so much confusion about who the Antichrist is?
On this reading, for two reasons: different biblical figures are merged into one composite person, and figures meant for the first century are moved into our future.

Popular teaching takes Daniel's little horn and "prince who is to come", Jesus's "abomination of desolation", Paul's "man of lawlessness", John's "antichrist" and Revelation's "beast". It then treats them all as one man. Yet these come from different books, with different settings and descriptions. The first error creates a figure no single text describes. The second error concerns time. Many of these texts speak of things near to their readers. Daniel's seventy weeks led to Messiah (Daniel 9:24-27), Jesus spoke of "this generation" (Matthew 24:34), and John spoke of "the last hour" (1 John 2:18). Sorting each figure by its own text and time clears much of the confusion.
Matthew 24:34: "This generation will not pass away until all these things are accomplished" (WEB).
1 John 2:18 places the antichrists in the readers' own "last hour".

Futurists argue that the shared features (blasphemy, war on the saints, a set time, self-exaltation) show that these texts describe one person from different angles. Many amillennial scholars also see a single final figure. They link the little horn, the man of lawlessness and the beast.
What does the popular "composite" Antichrist look like, and where do its parts come from?
It joins a European or Jewish ruler, a ten-nation league, a seven-year peace treaty with Israel, a faked resurrection, worship in a rebuilt temple and a 666 mark into one story.

The modern picture runs like this. After the rapture, a charming leader rises from a revived Roman Empire of ten nations (Daniel 7:7-8, 24). He subdues three rulers, then speaks of peace (Daniel 8:25; 1 Thessalonians 5:3). He makes a seven-year treaty with Israel and breaks it halfway (Daniel 9:27). He recovers from a deadly head wound (Revelation 13:3), sits in a rebuilt temple claiming to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4), and marks everyone with 666. Some say he must be Jewish because the beast comes from the "land" (Revelation 13:11). Others say he is Gentile because he comes from the "sea" (Isaiah 57:20). The fulfilled reading notes how much detail is built from scattered verses, many of which are ripped from their settings.
In the 1960s some saw John F. Kennedy as a candidate because of his head wound. This shows how easily the composite absorbs events.
Hitler's speech of 23 March 1933, which promised friendly relations with the Church, is cited by some as a model of the "man of peace".

Dispensational scholars defend the composite as careful synthesis, not invention. They argue that Daniel 7, 9 and 11, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 13 share specific features that point to one end-time ruler. They say this is how Scripture interprets Scripture.
Will the Antichrist arise from a revived ten-nation Roman Empire?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Daniel's fourth beast was the Roman Empire of the first century, and its "ten horns" belonged to that era, when Christ's kingdom came.

Daniel 2 and 7 describe four kingdoms. In the days of those kings, God sets up a kingdom that will never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). The fourth kingdom, strong as iron, is commonly identified as Rome. Christ came, preached that the kingdom was at hand (Mark 1:15), and received dominion from the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13-14; Matthew 28:18). This was during the Roman Empire, not a future revived one. Futurists must insert a gap of many centuries between the legs and the toes of Daniel's statue, or between the beast and its horns. The fulfilled reading sees no textual sign of such a gap. Attempts to match the ten horns to the European Common Market (which later grew past ten members) have failed.
Daniel 2:44: "In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom" (WEB).
The European Economic Community reached ten members in 1981, then twelve in 1986. Predictions based on "ten" were quietly dropped.

Dispensationalists hold that the ten-horn stage has not yet occurred, since no ten kings ruled at once in ancient Rome and Christ has not yet crushed the nations. Amillennial scholars often see the horns as symbolic of powers through history. Some see Daniel's fourth kingdom as Greece rather than Rome.
Does Scripture predict that the Antichrist will make a seven-year peace treaty with Israel?
Not on the fulfilled reading. Daniel 9:27 speaks of the Messiah confirming a covenant and ending sacrifice. No verse mentions a treaty with Antichrist.

The popular view rests on Daniel 9:27: "he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week". It takes "he" as a future ruler. But the nearest main subject in 9:26 is "Messiah", who is cut off. "The prince who is to come" is mentioned only as owner of the "people" who destroy the city. The fulfilled and many Reformed readings see the Messiah confirming the covenant (compare Matthew 26:28, "the blood of the new covenant ... for many"). In the middle of the week his death makes sacrifice and offering cease in God's sight. Daniel speaks of "confirming" a covenant, not of making a new treaty, and nothing about breaking it. The seven-year treaty is an inference, not a text.
Matthew 26:28: Jesus's blood "of the new covenant, which is poured out for many" (WEB). Note the echo of "many" in Daniel 9:27.
Hebrews 10:12-18: after Christ's one sacrifice, "there is no more offering for sin" (WEB).

Dispensational scholars argue that the nearest antecedent of "he" is "the prince who is to come" (9:26). They note that Christ did not literally stop temple sacrifices in AD 30. They read 9:27 with Daniel 11:31 and Matthew 24:15 as a future ruler who desecrates a temple.
Will a future Antichrist seem to rise from a deadly head wound and amaze the world?
On the fulfilled reading, the "wound that was healed" belongs to the beast's heads in John's day: Rome's near collapse after Nero's death and its revival under Vespasian.

Popular teaching says the Antichrist will suffer a mortal head wound, recover, and become an object of worship (Revelation 13:3-8). Hal Lindsey thought it would be a near-death recovery rather than a true resurrection. Modern audiences, used to stage illusions, would likely doubt such a show. More important is the text itself: one of the beast's seven heads was wounded, and the beast's deadly wound was healed. In 17:10 the heads are kings, so the wound fits the empire's crisis. When Nero died in AD 68, Rome fell into civil war under three short-lived emperors. Many expected the end of the empire. Vespasian restored it in AD 69. The world "marvelled" at Rome's survival.
Tacitus, Histories 1.11 and 2-3, describes the empire torn apart in AD 69 before Vespasian's victory.
Revelation 13:3: "one of his heads looked like it had been wounded fatally" (WEB). It is a head that is wounded, while the beast itself lives.

Futurists expect a future ruler's apparent death and recovery, imitating Christ's resurrection. Some scholars link the wound to the "Nero redivivus" legend. Idealists read it as evil powers that seem defeated but rise again in new forms.
Where does the word "antichrist" appear in the Bible, and what does it mean there?
Only in John's letters: 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; and 2 John 7. There an antichrist is anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.

The word "antichrist" is found in only four verses, all by John. An antichrist is "the liar" who denies that Jesus is the Christ (1 John 2:22). He denies the Father and the Son (2:22-23). Every spirit that does not confess Jesus is the spirit of antichrist (4:3). Many deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh are "the deceiver and the antichrist" (2 John 7). B. B. Warfield noted that for John this was a denial of the Incarnation. To deny that Jesus is the Christ was to deny that he is God's Son come in the flesh. As a result, John's antichrist is a false teacher, not a world dictator. What these passages teach is the whole New Testament teaching on "antichrist" by name.
2 John 7: "many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who don't confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh" (WEB).
Docetists in the late first century taught that Christ only seemed to have a body. Ignatius of Antioch opposed them (To the Smyrnaeans 2).

Most scholars agree on what John's letters say. Many futurists and amillennialists also hold that John's "antichrist is coming" shows that the church expected one final figure. They link him with the man of lawlessness and the beast. Those figures are described with other words.
Is the biblical antichrist a political ruler or a religious deceiver?
In John's usage, a religious deceiver. Antichrists are teachers and spirits who deny the truth about Christ. They are not political rulers, however hostile to Christ.

John's antichrists "went out from us" (1 John 2:19). They had once been inside the Christian community and left it. They are "false prophets" (4:1) and "deceivers" (2 John 7). Their crime is false teaching about the person of Christ. Nothing in John's letters speaks of armies, treaties, economies or worldwide rule. On this reading, the modern composite figure, a charming statesman ruling the world, is not the antichrist of 1 and 2 John. A political leader may oppose Christ, but John's term names a system of apostasy and the people who teach it. Jesus foretold the same: many would fall away, and false prophets would arise and deceive many (Matthew 24:10-11).
1 John 2:19: "They went out from us, but they didn't belong to us" (WEB). These are former insiders.
Matthew 24:11: "Many false prophets will arise, and will lead many astray" (WEB).

Futurists accept that John's antichrists were false teachers. They argue that the final Antichrist will combine false religion and political power, as with the beast and false prophet of Revelation 13. Historicists saw the papacy as uniting both roles.
Is there one antichrist or many?
John says "many antichrists have arisen". He seems to correct a popular idea of one coming figure by pointing to the many false teachers already present.

John writes: "you heard that the antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have arisen" (1 John 2:18). Warfield suggested that John was taking a current belief and reshaping it. His readers had "heard" of one Antichrist, but John points them to the reality: many antichrists. He does the same in his Gospel, where he corrects a rumour that he would not die before the Lord returned (John 21:22-23). Jesus also corrected what people had "heard" from tradition (Matthew 5:21-43). On this reading, the many antichrists are the false Christs and false prophets that Jesus foretold would arise before Jerusalem fell (Matthew 24:24). They were present in John's own day.
John 21:23: "This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that this disciple wouldn't die. Yet Jesus didn't say..." (WEB). John corrects a rumour.
Matthew 5:21-22: "You have heard ... but I tell you". Jesus reshapes what hearers had been taught.

Many interpreters, including many amillennialists and futurists, read 1 John 2:18 as both/and: many antichrists now, and one final Antichrist still to come. They take John's words as confirming the expectation of a final antichrist, not correcting it.
What did John mean by "it is the last hour"?
He meant his own time. Antichrists had already arisen, "by which we know it is the last hour". On this reading, it was the last hour of the old covenant age before AD 70.

John says twice in one verse that it is the last hour, and gives proof: many antichrists have arisen (1 John 2:18). The proof was visible to his readers, so the hour was theirs. Jesus had told his disciples, John among them, that their generation would see the temple destroyed and that false Christs would arise first (Matthew 24:5, 24, 34). On this reading, John wrote near the time of that fulfilment. He saw in the rising false teachers a sign that the end of the age was close. Other writers used similar words. The ends of the ages had come on them (1 Corinthians 10:11), and Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26).
Hebrews 9:26: Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin (WEB). This is in the past tense for the writer.
Matthew 24:5, 24: false christs and false prophets were warned of before the temple's fall.

Many scholars read the "last hour" as the whole period between Christ's first and second comings. They say it began at the resurrection and continues until he returns. On this view, every generation lives in the last hour, though the final end is still future.
Was there a great apostasy in the first century?
Yes. The New Testament records widespread false teaching and falling away before AD 70, as Jesus foretold.

False teaching arose almost at once. Paul opposed "a different gospel" (Galatians 1:6-9) and false brothers (2:4). He warned the Ephesian elders that men would rise from among them to draw away disciples (Acts 20:29-30). Some said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), and others denied it (1 Corinthians 15:12). Some banned marriage and foods (1 Timothy 4:1-3). Paul could say that "all who are in Asia" had turned away from him (2 Timothy 1:15). Hebrews warns a whole community on the edge of turning back. Revelation 2-3 names false apostles, the teaching of Balaam, the Nicolaitans and "Jezebel". Jesus had foretold this: many would fall away and false prophets would deceive (Matthew 24:10-12).
2 Timothy 1:15: "all who are in Asia turned away from me" (WEB).
Revelation 2:2: the church in Ephesus tested those who called themselves apostles and found them false.

Futurists agree that apostasy was present then. They hold that Paul's "the falling away" (2 Thessalonians 2:3) is a distinct, final apostasy before Christ's return. They see current trends in the church as possible signs of it.
Why does the word "antichrist" never appear in Revelation?
Even though John wrote both the letters and Revelation (on the traditional view), he never calls the beast "antichrist". This suggests they are different ideas.

The same John who defines antichrist in his letters wrote Revelation, by early tradition. Yet the word "antichrist" is absent from the Apocalypse. Commentators have noted how striking this is, since the word was typical of John's circle and would have suited several passages. If the beast of Revelation 13 were the antichrist of 1 John, we might expect John to use his own term. The fulfilled reading draws a simple conclusion. John used "antichrist" for false teachers who denied the Incarnation, and "beast" for the persecuting power of Rome and its allies. Popular teaching joins them, but John kept them apart.
Revelation uses "beast" (thērion) over thirty times, and "antichrist" not once.
1 John uses "antichrist" for teachers who "went out from us", a different kind of figure from a ruling empire.

Many scholars hold that the letters and Revelation may come from different Johns, so vocabulary need not match. Futurists argue that the beast is the final fulfilment of what John called "the antichrist" who was "coming". In this view the ideas are related, though described with different words.
